newsitem.title: UK: British business leaders blast tube underfunding.
newsitem.headline: British business leaders blast tube underfunding.

text.p: Britain's business leaders are set to blast the government's inadequate funding of the London Underground metro system in a letter obtained by Reuters on Wednesday, warning of dangers to the capital's businesses and its tourist industry.
Chief executives of six nationwide Chambers of Commerce have joined forces in an unprecedented attack on the underfunding of the 'Tube', just weeks ahead of a British election on May 1.

The group, which is one of Britain's most powerful voices in the business community, said: "It is important to the whole country to ensure that London's Tube network is not in an embarrassing state of decay with frequent disruption, overcrowding, delays and unreliability."

The attack coincides with calls by the ruling Conservative Party for the privatisation of the network and with the Labour party pledging to solve the crisis through public-private partnership projects.

Bosses of the Liverpool, Manchester, North-East England, Bristol, Glasgow and Edinburgh Chambers of Commerce made a public plea for more cash to be injected into London's metro in a letter due to be published by the Financial Times on Thursday.
The chambers, which represent 15,000 businesses, say in the letter they feared the crumbling network would mean less new investment in Britain's capital and less tourist income.

"As members of the national network of approved Chambers of Commerce, we are concerned about the likely future deterioration of the London Underground system following a reduction in London Transport's investment," they said in the letter.

Andrew Hawkins, director of policy at the London Chamber of Commerce, told a conference in London earlier the Tube was crucial to London's economy, which is the economic engine for the rest of Britain. He said London represented one fifth of the nation's total GDP.

"London's economy has an annual output of 160 billion pounds ($260.1 billion) a year," he said. "That's bigger than any of the Scandinavian countries and three and a half times that of Ireland. So it's not hard to see how the cost of congestion in the capital can be upwards of 10 billion pounds," said Hawkins.
He said London faced the threat of losing money first through delays due to a transport gridlock in the capital hindering movement of goods and people.
Also it weighed against the capital in terms of global competitiveness to attract new investment into London as opposed to Frankfurt, New York or Tokyo. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
